titre: The Scandal of The Rite of Spring Was Not a Riot
accroche: The audience shouts so loudly that the orchestra can no longer be heard. Then the dancers take five bows, and the program continues as normal.
contenu_vulgarise:
On May 29, 1913, at the Théâtre des Champs-Élysées in Paris, Sergei Diaghilev's Ballets Russes premiere *Le Sacre du printemps* (The Rite of Spring), a ballet by Igor Stravinsky on a scenario imagined by the painter and archaeologist Nicholas Roerich: the ritual sacrifice of a young girl to the god of spring. The score, of an unprecedented rhythmic violence, had already required more than one hundred thirty dance rehearsals and seventeen orchestra rehearsals, an exceptional number for the time. Conductor Pierre Monteux, on discovering the piano reduction, would confide that he thought Stravinsky had gone mad.

Vaslav Nijinsky's choreography breaks just as completely with tradition: feet turned inward, knees bent, heavy and angular gestures where classical ballet calls for lightness and curved lines. From the first bars, the house divides. The booing soon drowns out the orchestra, to the point that Nijinsky, perched on a chair in the wings, has to shout the cues to the dancers to be heard over the din.

## What the witnesses of the time really tell

The story has come down under the name “the Rite of Spring riot,” with its train of brawls between spectators and police intervention. Neither of these two elements is attested by the accounts of the time. Two days after the premiere, the critic Gaston de Pawlowski writes in *Comœdia* that one had to “strain one's ear amid an indescribable uproar” to guess at the work, drowned in equal parts under the cries of its supporters and its opponents, but he mentions no blows exchanged.

A still firmer clue: the dancers take five bows at the end of the ballet, before the program continues normally with another piece. A genuine riot would hardly have allowed such continuity. The word “riot” moreover only appears in the accounts from the 1920s on, used as an advertising argument to draw American audiences to performances of the work.

## What it shifts

What really happened that evening looks less like a riot than like a noisy, passionate but nonviolent scuffle between supporters and opponents of a work that deliberately broke with all the conventions of ballet. The myth of the riot ended up distorting history in the direction one prefers to give it, that of an art so radical that it literally drove the audience off its hinges. The documented reality is more modest, and the score, for its part, won its place without needing any brawl to do so.

citation.texte: It was therefore, straining our ears, amid an indescribable uproar that we had, painfully, to form an approximate idea of the new work, equally prevented from hearing it by its defenders and its opponents.

carte.punch: The audience shouts so loudly that the orchestra can no longer be heard. Then the dancers take five bows.
carte.idee: In 1913, the premiere of The Rite of Spring sets off an uproar so loud that Nijinsky has to shout his cues from the wings. But the dancers take five bows and the program continues: nothing attests to the brawl that the legend has told since the 1920s.

quiz.question: Which element, reported by contemporary accounts of the premiere of The Rite of Spring, contradicts the story of a genuine riot?
choix: The police, called to the scene, drew up no report that evening
The dancers took five bows at the end of the ballet, before the program continued normally
Stravinsky himself publicly denied any violence the very next day
The theater reopened with no repairs in the following days
quiz.explication: The firmest point against the riot story is that the dancers took five bows at the end of the performance and that the program continued normally with another piece: a real riot would hardly have allowed such continuity. No account of the time mentions police intervention or damage to the theater.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Who conceived the scenario of The Rite of Spring, on which Stravinsky composed his music?
choix: Nicholas Roerich, painter and archaeologist, author of the scenario about the ritual sacrifice of a young girl
Sergei Diaghilev, the director of the Ballets Russes who produced the show
Pierre Monteux, the conductor who led the premiere
Gaston de Pawlowski, the critic who reviewed the evening in Comœdia
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The scenario, the ritual sacrifice of a young girl to the god of spring, is the work of the painter and archaeologist Nicholas Roerich, distinct from Diaghilev the producer and Monteux the conductor.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does Nijinsky do during the performance, because of the uproar drowning out the orchestra?
choix: He interrupts the show to ask the audience for calm
He signals Monteux to stop the orchestra until the booing ends
He leaves the wings to harangue the audience from the stage
He shouts the cues to the dancers from a chair, in the wings, to be heard
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Perched on a chair in the wings, Nijinsky has to shout the choreographic cues to the dancers to cover the din of the house, without ever interrupting the performance.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What made the score of The Rite of Spring so hard to stage, even before the premiere evening?
choix: Stravinsky delivered the score several months behind the planned schedule
Its unprecedented rhythmic violence required more than one hundred thirty dance rehearsals and seventeen orchestra rehearsals
The theater's orchestra at first refused to play music judged too modern
Nijinsky had to rewrite the choreography entirely two weeks before the premiere
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The score's unprecedented rhythmic violence required an exceptional number of rehearsals for the time, more than one hundred thirty for dance and seventeen for orchestra, even before the premiere.
